scope_allowed: Relevance of the quantities of interest

models.name: HF-Contact
models.what_it_computes: Implicit finite element model resolving frictional pin–cortex contact, clamp interfaces, and bar–clamp compliance to predict construct stiffness under prescribed loads.

models.name: RB-Beam
models.what_it_computes: Implicit finite element reduced-order model using beam/spring idealization of bars and pins with rigid connectors to predict construct stiffness under prescribed loads.

mechanisms.name: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Determines interfragmentary motion magnitude along the load axis, influencing callus formation and early stability.

mechanisms.name: Frontal-plane bending (varus–valgus) about the fracture gap
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Controls shear and opening/closing across the gap during mediolateral loading, which affects alignment maintenance and tissue strain environment.

deviation.detail: All factor scores are reported on a 0–5 Credibility Index (CI) per model–mechanism pair, with acceptance defined as CI ≥ 3.0 for the stated medium model risk.

expected_decision.outcome_source: Under ASME V&V 40 with a declared medium model risk and a private 0–5 CI scale, both HF-Contact and RB-Beam achieved acceptable credibility for predicting construct stiffness of a modular unilateral tibial external fixator under axial compression and frontal-plane bending.

expected_context_of_use: The context of use (CoU) is to support design verification and preclinical evidence planning; model outputs inform design iteration and bench test priorities but do not directly infer clinical performance.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: For HF-Contact under axial compression, stiffness values for coarse, medium, and fine meshes were 303, 309, and 311 N/mm, respectively.
The extrapolated infinite-resolution value was 312 N/mm with a Grid Convergence Index (GCI) on the fine mesh of 1.6% at a 95% confidence factor.
HF-Contact’s finest practical meshes produced grid-convergence indices below 1.6% (axial) and 2.4% (bending).
findings.span: For HF-Contact under axial compression, stiffness values for coarse, medium, and fine meshes were 303, 309, and 311 N/mm, respectively.

findings.mechanism: Frontal-plane bending (varus–valgus) about the fracture gap
spans: For frontal-plane bending, rotational stiffnesses were 2120, 2140, and 2152 N·mm/deg, with an extrapolated value of 2158 N·mm/deg and a fine-mesh GCI of 2.4%.
HF-Contact’s finest practical meshes produced grid-convergence indices below 1.6% (axial) and 2.4% (bending).
findings.span: For frontal-plane bending, rotational stiffnesses were 2120, 2140, and 2152 N·mm/deg, with an extrapolated value of 2158 N·mm/deg and a fine-mesh GCI of 2.4%.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: In HF-Contact, the difference between measured and modeled bar bending stiffness was held within 2.2%, and clamp rotational response was within 3.4% of the mean of component tests.
Measured bar modulus (68.5 GPa) and geometric dimensions were used directly, and clamp joint behavior was inferred from component tests.
findings.span: In HF-Contact, the difference between measured and modeled bar bending stiffness was held within 2.2%, and clamp rotational response was within 3.4% of the mean of component tests.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: Within HF-Contact, contact enforcement was verified by matching normal approach and contact pressure to analytical predictions for smooth convex bodies at low loads (small strains), giving <1.2% relative error at the finest mesh density.

Frictional tangential response was compared to Cattaneo–Mindlin behavior qualitatively through load–unload loops at low slip; the observed stick–slip transition in the code was consistent with expectations.
Code-oriented checks reproduced linear elastic and Hertzian contact benchmarks within 0.5–1.2%.
findings.span: Within HF-Contact, contact enforcement was verified by matching normal approach and contact pressure to analytical predictions for smooth convex bodies at low loads (small strains), giving <1.2% relative error at the finest mesh density.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: At each increment, we verify that the ratio of the residual force norm to the external load norm falls below 10^-8 and that the displacement correction norm stabilizes.
Contact penetration is monitored as the maximum normal approach at the pin–cortex interface and kept below 3 µm at the final increments.

Tightening the force residual tolerance by one 6 xator stiffness FEA order of magnitude and halving the maximum increment size led to changes in axial stiffness of 0.1% and in bending rotational stiffness of 0.2%.
findings.span: At each increment, we verify that the ratio of the residual force norm to the external load norm falls below 10^-8 and that the displacement correction norm stabilizes.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: The mean axial stiffness across eight builds was 302 N/mm with a standard deviation of 18 N/mm, giving a coefficient of variation of 6.0%.

Eight physical constructs per mechanism (five repeated assemblies and three manufactured duplicates) were tested; coefficients of variation were 6–8%, with controlled fixture alignment and clamp torque.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: For RB-Beam, axial stiffness was 291, 294, and 295 N/mm for 2, 5, and 10 elements per member, respectively, with an extrapolated value of 296 N/mm and a fine-mesh GCI of 0.7%.
The RB-Beam refinement sequence converged faster in terms of global compliance, with 0.7% and 1.1% uncertainty for axial and bending stiffness, respectively, at 10 elements per member.

findings.mechanism: Axial compression across a standardized fracture gap
spans: In RB-Beam, spring values tuned to match component-level torsional response reached within 5.0% of measured values, and beam properties reconstructed the measured bar bending stiffness within 1.6%.

Effective pin–cortex engagement length was set at 22 mm based on sur-rogate sectioning; the resulting axial slip stiffness in RB-Beam, 55 kN/mm, reproduced observed load–displacement response within 4.7% under isolated pin loading.
findings.span: In RB-Beam, spring values tuned to match component-level torsional response reached within 5.0% of measured values, and beam properties reconstructed the measured bar bending stiffness within 1.6%.

spans: The residuals are at machine precision for the problem scales considered, and constraint equations enforced by rigid connectors are satisfied to within 10^-12 m or rad.
The QoIs were unchanged at the third significant figure when spring stiffnesses were varied within a factor of two around their calibrated values.
In RB-Beam, which solves linearly in one step, constraints were satisfied to within 10^-12 and QoIs were unchanged to three significant figures when spring values were perturbed by a factor of two.

findings.factor: Relevance of the quantities of interest
spans: The primary outputs are linearized construct stiffness under standardized loads: axial stiffness in N/mm from the slope of the load–displacement response over the 50–500 N interval and rotational stiffness in N·mm/deg from the slope of the moment– angle response over the 1–7.5 N·m interval in frontal-plane bending.
These outputs map directly to design verification criteria employed in our internal test protocols, both in form and in reporting practice.
The reported outputs correspond exactly to the metrics used in design verification, expressed in N/mm and N·mm/deg under the same fixtures and load application points.
